scenarios.title: Scenario 5 — Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenarios.domains: D3 Claude Code Configuration · D4 Prompt Engineering · D2 Tool Design & MCP
scenarios.brief: A health-records software company runs Claude Code headlessly in GitLab CI on a Python and TypeScript monorepo of 14 services, about 300 merge requests a week. Workloads: a merge-request review that posts inline comments, test generation for changed modules, an autofix job for failing lint and unit tests, and a post-merge migration scan. Review findings are emitted with --output-format json and --json-schema. CLAUDE.md and .claude/ are committed to the repository.

scenarios.title: Scenario 6 — Structured Data Extraction
scenarios.domains: D4 Prompt Engineering · D1 Agentic Architecture · D5 Context & Reliability
scenarios.brief: A commercial real-estate firm abstracts lease packets into its lease-administration system. A packet holds a base lease (20–140 pages, text-layer PDF), zero or more amendments, and sometimes side letters and guaranties. An Agent SDK coordinator extracts parties, term dates, rent schedule, escalations, renewal options and security deposit through tool use with JSON schemas, validates with Pydantic, and posts the abstract. Volume is about 1,200 packets a month; paralegals handle exceptions.

questions.question: The review job links findings to tickets through the tracker vendor's community MCP server. A staff engineer set it up by adding the server to the user-level Claude Code config in the runner image, credential included, and last week the registry's image scanner flagged that credential as exposed. When a review run behaves oddly, the on-call engineer reproduces it by checking out the branch on a laptop and running the same command; the tracker tools are missing there, so reproductions rarely match CI. What is the best change?

options.t: Keep the server in the runner's ~/.claude.json, delete the stored secret from the image, and inject it from the CI secret store at job start.
options.why: Runner-up. This clears the scanner finding and would be the right fix if only the runner used the server. User-level config does not travel with a checkout, so the laptop reproduction still lacks the tools.

options.t: Register the server in the job's setup step with claude mcp add --scope user, passing the secret from the CI secret store as an argument.
options.why: Incorrect. Registering at user scope on each run keeps the secret out of the image but is still per-machine; a laptop checkout gets nothing.

options.t: Add the server to a committed .claude/settings.local.json, with the secret read from an environment variable when Claude Code starts.
options.why: Incorrect. settings.local.json is the personal, uncommitted settings file and is not where shared MCP servers are declared; the shared home is .mcp.json.

options.t: Move the definition into a .mcp.json at the repository root, with the credential written as ${TRACKER_TOKEN} and supplied by CI or the laptop.
options.why: Correct. Project-scope .mcp.json is version-controlled, so any checkout gets the server, and env var expansion keeps the secret out of both the repository and the image.

questions.decider: The on-call engineer reproduces from a plain checkout, so the server must travel with the repository; if only the runner used it, user-level config with an injected secret would be enough.
questions.explanation: Shared MCP servers belong in project-level .mcp.json; personal or experimental ones in ~/.claude.json. Environment variable expansion lets a committed config carry no secret.

eli5.question: Where should a shared tool connection be written down so that everyone who copies the project gets it? The leaked token is loud, but it is not the deciding fact. The clue is: the on-call engineer checks out the branch on a laptop, and the tracker tools are missing there.
eli5.answer: Think of a shared office recipe book versus a note in one cook's pocket. The recipe book travels with the kitchen; the pocket note stays with one person. A committed .mcp.json is the recipe book (the project-scope MCP config), so every checkout gets the tool. Writing the token as ${TRACKER_TOKEN} (environment variable expansion) means the book names the key but never contains it. Rule: shared tool, shared file; secrets go in as ${VARS}, never as values.
options: Runner-up. This takes the key out of the cook's pocket note, which fixes the leak. It would win if only the CI runner needed the tool. A laptop checkout still has no note.
This writes the pocket note fresh on each CI run (user scope). The secret is safer, but the laptop still gets nothing.
settings.local.json is meant to be your personal, uncommitted settings file. It is also not where shared MCP servers are declared.
Correct. The project's own .mcp.json travels with every checkout, and the token is filled in from each machine's environment.

questions.question: The autofix job must raise a timeout constant in client_factory.py, for the payments client only. The agent's Edit call returns an error saying the target text matches three locations, and the log shows it reissuing that Edit. The file is codegen output: a template emits one 60-line retry helper per client class, identical apart from the class declaration that precedes each copy, and the constant sits near the middle of the helper. The payments client is the second of three. What should the agent do next?

options.t: Lengthen old_string with neighbouring lines above and below the constant until it identifies exactly one place, then reissue the Edit.
options.why: Runner-up. Widening the anchor is the usual cure for a non-unique match and would win if the copies differed near the constant. Here the bodies are identical for 60 lines, so no nearby context is unique.

options.t: Use Grep in line-number mode to locate the second occurrence, then pass that line number to Edit along with the replacement value.
options.why: Incorrect. Edit works by unique text match, not by line number, so locating the line does not make the match unique.

options.t: Load the complete file contents, change the value in the payments copy alone, and save the entire file back with the Write tool.
options.why: Correct. When Edit cannot find a unique anchor, the fallback is Read followed by Write of the whole file with the targeted change.

options.t: Change the timeout in the generator's template instead, then rerun the codegen step to regenerate client_factory.py from it.
options.why: Incorrect. The template emits every client, so the change would reach all three, not only payments.

questions.decider: The three helpers are identical for their whole 60-line body; if the text around the constant differed per copy, widening old_string would be the better move.
questions.explanation: Edit makes targeted changes through a unique text match. When no unique anchor exists, Read the file and Write it back with the change.

eli5.question: The edit tool keeps failing because the text it is told to change appears three times. What should the agent do instead? The clue is: the three copies are identical for their whole 60-line body, apart from the class line above each.
eli5.answer: Picture find-and-replace in a document where the same paragraph is printed three times. If you can't describe which copy you mean, find-and-replace can't help. So you open the whole document, change the one copy by hand, and save it (Read, then Write). Edit works only when the text you point at is unique; that is the fallback the exam guide names. Rule: if Edit can't find a unique match, Read the whole file and Write it back.
options: Runner-up. Adding nearby lines is the normal way to make a match unique. It would win if the copies differed near the constant. Here they are identical for 60 lines.
Edit does not accept a line number; it matches text. Knowing the line does not make the text unique.
Correct. Load the whole file, change only the payments copy, and save it back. This is the fallback when Edit has no unique anchor.
The template prints all three clients, so changing it changes all three. Only payments should change.

questions.question: Migration conventions (no column drop without a two-release deprecation; indexes built concurrently) are a section of the root CLAUDE.md, now 600 lines and loaded on every review. Roughly four in five merge requests touch no migration. Each service owns its schema history next to its code, as in services/billing/db/migrations/ and services/claims/db/migrations/, fourteen in all. Reviewers say the concurrency rule is missed most often on long diffs. Where should these conventions live?

options.t: In a CLAUDE.md placed in each service's schema-history folder, with a CI job that fails if the fourteen copies drift apart.
options.why: Runner-up. A directory CLAUDE.md loads only where it sits and would be the natural home if all schema history lived in one folder. Across fourteen folders it means fourteen copies to keep in step.

options.t: In a file under .claude/rules/ whose paths: frontmatter globs services/*/db/migrations/**, removed from the root file.
options.why: Correct. A glob-scoped rule loads only for matching files, wherever they sit, so one file covers all fourteen services and stays out of the reviews that touch none.

options.t: In a project skill under .claude/skills/ that the review prompt invokes by name whenever the diff includes a schema change.
options.why: Incorrect. Skills are on-demand workflows; this relies on the prompt deciding when to load conventions that a path rule attaches to the files automatically.

options.t: In a separate docs/migrations.md pulled into the root file with @import and placed at the top under its own heading.
options.why: Incorrect. Better placement may help on long diffs, but imported content still loads on every review, including the four in five with no migration.

questions.decider: The schema folders are spread across fourteen services; if they all sat in one folder, a directory CLAUDE.md there would serve as well.
questions.explanation: .claude/rules/ files with paths: globs load conventions only for matching files and beat directory CLAUDE.md when those files span many directories. @import organises content but does not make it conditional.

eli5.question: Where should rules about database migrations live so they appear only when a migration is being reviewed? The "missed on long diffs" remark is a distraction. The clue is: migrations sit in fourteen separate service folders, and four in five reviews touch none.
eli5.answer: Think of a library sticker that says "handle with gloves" put on every rare book, wherever it is shelved. A path-scoped rule in .claude/rules/ with a paths: glob is that sticker: it loads only when matching files are involved. One file covers all fourteen folders, and reviews without migrations never load it. Rule: conventions for files spread across many folders go in a .claude/rules/ file with paths:.
options: Runner-up. A folder-level CLAUDE.md loads only in its own folder. It would win if all migrations were in one folder; here you would keep fourteen copies in sync.
Correct. One rule file with a glob matching every service's migration folder loads only when those files are in play.
A skill is a workflow you call on demand. Here the prompt would have to decide when to load conventions that a path rule attaches automatically.
An @import organises the file, but imported text still loads on every review, including the ones with no migrations.

questions.question: Developers and the release job both draft the changelog with a 60-line procedure: walk the git log since the last tag, group commits by service, and fetch each linked ticket's title. It lives in the root CLAUDE.md, which every review run also loads. Run interactively, it prints around 4,000 lines of log into the session, and developers say Claude's later answers in that session start missing details from earlier work. The release manager wants changes to the procedure reviewed in merge requests like code. Which home fits best?

options.t: A project command file at .claude/commands/changelog.md, invoked as a slash command from CI and from interactive sessions.
options.why: Runner-up. A project command is shared, versioned and on demand, and would be enough if the procedure produced little output. It runs inside the current conversation, so the log still floods it.

options.t: A rule under .claude/rules/ with paths: ["docs/changelog.md"], loading the procedure only while that file is being edited.
options.why: Incorrect. Path rules carry conventions for matching files; they do not isolate a procedure's output, and the log still lands in the session.

options.t: The root file, with a line handing the git-log walk to the Explore subagent and asking it to return a grouped summary.
options.why: Incorrect. Delegation would isolate the output, but the procedure stays in a file every review run loads.

options.t: A SKILL.md under .claude/skills/changelog/ whose frontmatter sets context: fork, called from CI and interactive sessions.
options.why: Correct. A project skill is versioned and loaded on demand, and context: fork runs it in an isolated sub-agent context, keeping the log out of the main conversation.

questions.decider: The procedure's output degrades the developer's session and the root file loads on every review; with little output, a project command would serve equally well.
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md holds always-loaded standards; skills are on-demand workflows, and context: fork runs one in an isolated sub-agent context.

eli5.question: Where should a long, noisy changelog procedure live? The clue is: running it dumps about 4,000 lines into the session, and the root file it sits in loads on every review.
eli5.answer: Imagine sending a helper to the archive room to sort old letters. They come back with one neat summary, not a cartful of paper on your desk. A project skill with context: fork works like that: it runs in its own side room (an isolated sub-agent context) and keeps the log out of your conversation. It sits in .claude/skills/, so it is versioned and loads only when called. Rule: an on-demand workflow with noisy output belongs in a skill with context: fork.
options: Runner-up. A project command is shared and on demand. It would win if the procedure printed little. It runs in your conversation, so the 4,000 lines still land there.
Path rules carry conventions for matching files. They do not run a procedure in a separate room, so the log still lands in the session.
Handing the work to the Explore subagent would keep the log out, but the procedure stays in a file every review loads.
Correct. A versioned skill that runs in its own isolated context, called only when needed.

questions.question: A nightly job asks Claude Code to fix a currency-rounding helper that is a cent off for some locales, after a customer reported a wrong invoice total in Swiss francs. The helper's module ships with a parametrized pytest file of 140 cases; 23 are red on main, and the job's container has the project's dev dependencies installed. The job runs with -p overnight, unattended, and the fix touches one function. How should the prompt be structured to reach a correct fix most reliably?

options.t: Have Claude run the module's suite, change the code against the reported failures, and loop until no case is failing.
options.why: Correct. Test-driven iteration uses the existing failing cases as specification and feedback, and the full suite catches regressions in other locales.

options.t: Give Claude several worked amounts with locale and expected rounded output, including the Swiss franc invoice, inside the prompt.
options.why: Runner-up. Concrete input/output pairs beat prose and would be the best choice if no runnable suite existed. Here 140 executable cases already exist, and a handful of pairs cannot catch a regression.

options.t: Open by having Claude ask its clarifying questions about the rounding rules before it proposes any change to the code.
options.why: Incorrect. The interview pattern needs someone to answer, and an unattended overnight run has nobody.

options.t: Start in plan mode, letting Claude explore the rounding code and propose an approach before making any modification.
options.why: Incorrect. Plan mode suits large or architectural changes; a one-function fix gains little, and an unattended run has nobody to approve a plan.

questions.decider: A runnable 140-case suite is available in the job's container; without it, concrete input/output pairs in the prompt would be the strongest option.
questions.explanation: Concrete examples and test-driven iteration both beat prose. When executable tests exist, iterating against them gives a verifiable stop condition.

eli5.question: How should an unattended overnight job be told to fix a rounding bug? The Swiss-franc invoice is the vivid detail. The clue is: a 140-case test file already exists, and the job's container can run it.
eli5.answer: Think of a recipe with a tasting panel standing by. Instead of describing the perfect cake in words, you bake, let the panel taste, adjust, and repeat until every taster is happy. The 140 tests are the panel (test-driven iteration). They also catch it when fixing one locale breaks another. Rule: if runnable tests exist, let Claude iterate against them.
options: Correct. Run the tests, fix against the failures, and repeat until nothing fails.
Runner-up. Concrete input-and-output pairs beat prose and would be best if no tests existed. A handful of pairs can't catch a regression the full suite would.
Asking questions first (the interview pattern) needs a person to answer. Nobody is watching an overnight job.
Plan mode is for big, multi-file or architectural changes. This is one function, and nobody is there to approve a plan.

questions.obj: 4.1 Explicit criteria for a retained category
questions.question: The reviewer's unhandled-error category produces about 40% of comments, and developers dismiss three in four. A manager's sample of 100 dismissed ones found two kinds: calls already wrapped by the service framework's error middleware, and errors re-raised on purpose to a caller that handles them. The category appears in the company's SOC 2 control matrix as an automated check run on every merge request. The prompt asks Claude to "flag missing or inadequate error handling". What is the most effective change?

options.t: Switch the category off in the review prompt while a rewritten version is tested against past merge requests, then restore it.
options.why: Runner-up. Pausing a noisy category to restore trust is sound and would win if it were optional. It is a listed control that must run on every merge request, so it has to be fixed in place.

options.t: Add a detected_pattern field to each finding and record dismissals against it, then tune the category from that data.
options.why: Incorrect. Pattern tracking finds unknown false-positive sources; the sample has already named both, so it delays the fix.

options.t: Redefine the check as an exception caught and dropped or a returned value left unused, with snippets on both sides.
options.why: Correct. Categorical criteria with concrete code cut false positives while the check keeps running.

options.t: Pass each finding in that category to a second, independent Claude instance that confirms or rejects it before it is posted.
options.why: Incorrect. An independent reviewer judging against the same vague definition inherits its ambiguity, at double the cost.

questions.decider: The category is a compliance control that must run on every merge request; if it could be paused, switching it off while it is rewritten would come first.
questions.explanation: Vague instructions produce false positives that erode trust. Replace them with categorical criteria and concrete code, not with more review layers.

eli5.question: A noisy review category annoys developers. How do you make it accurate? The angry dismissal numbers invite you to switch it off. The clue is: the category is a compliance control that must run on every merge request.
eli5.answer: Picture a smoke alarm that goes off whenever someone makes toast. You can't unplug it, because the fire code requires it. So you make it smarter about what counts as smoke. Here that means stating exactly what to flag, an error caught and thrown away or a result ignored, with short code samples on both sides (explicit categorical criteria). Rule: to cut false positives, define the category precisely; vague words breed noise.
options: Runner-up. Pausing a noisy check is a good way to win back trust. It would win if the check were optional. Compliance says it must keep running.
Tracking which patterns get dismissed (detected_pattern) helps find unknown causes. The manager's sample already found both causes.
Correct. Spell out what counts and what doesn't, with code on both sides. The check keeps running with far fewer false alarms.
A second reviewer using the same vague definition makes the same vague calls, at twice the cost.

questions.question: Findings come back through --json-schema with file, line, severity, issue and suggested_fix on every one, and parsing has not failed in a month. Developers act on about 20% of findings. Interviews show they act when the fix shows replacement code and ignore the rest; today a third of fixes read like "consider refactoring" and a few restate the issue. The prompt already describes the expected fix format in a paragraph. What is the most effective first step?

options.t: Turn suggested_fix in the schema into an object with required replacement_code and explanation strings.
options.why: Runner-up. Tightening the schema is right when fields are missing or mis-shaped. Every field already parses; a required string can still hold "consider refactoring".

options.t: Include three complete sample findings in the prompt, each with a code-level remedy, one spanning several lines.
options.why: Correct. When written instructions alone give inconsistent output, two to four targeted samples are the most effective way to get consistent, actionable content.

options.t: Check each fix for a code block before posting and, when one is missing, re-prompt with that finding and the element it lacks.
options.why: Incorrect. Retry-with-feedback is a sound safety net, but as a first step it pays for a second call on a third of findings instead of fixing the first output.

options.t: Send each finding to a second, independent Claude instance that rewrites its fix as replacement code before the comment is posted.
options.why: Incorrect. A rewriting pass doubles calls on every run to repair output the first pass can be shown how to produce.

questions.decider: Structure already validates and a written description of the format is in place; if fields were missing or mis-shaped, tightening the schema would come first.
questions.explanation: Schemas govern shape, not whether a field's content is useful. Few-shot samples are the strongest first lever for consistent, actionable content once instructions exist.

eli5.question: Every finding has the right fields, but many suggested fixes are vague. What should you try first? The clue is: parsing has not failed in a month, and a paragraph already describes the fix format.
eli5.answer: Think of training a new waiter. Telling them "describe the dish well" gets mixed results. Showing three good descriptions gets consistent ones. A form (the schema) makes sure each box exists; it can't make what's written in the box useful. A few complete samples in the prompt (few-shot examples) teach the content. Rule: a schema fixes shape; samples fix content.
options: Runner-up. A stricter schema helps when fields are missing or malformed. Here every field already parses, and a required string can still say "consider refactoring".
Correct. Three full sample findings with real code fixes show the model what "actionable" looks like.
Checking for code and retrying is a sound safety net. As a first step, it pays for a second call on a third of findings instead of fixing the first answer.
A rewriting pass doubles the calls to repair something the first pass can be shown how to do.

questions.question: The post-merge migration scan posts to the on-call channel and gates nothing. Finance wants it on the Message Batches API for the 50% discount, pointing out that three trial batches returned in under 20 minutes. On-call engineers read each scan before the next production deploy train, which leaves every 90 minutes, and pull a risky change from the train if needed. About 60 merges a day are scanned. How should the team evaluate the proposal?

options.t: Adopt the batch endpoint for the scan, one request per merged change, using its merge commit SHA as the custom_id for matching.
options.why: Runner-up. Non-blocking work correlated by custom_id is a textbook batch fit and would win if results were read the next day. Batches can take up to 24 hours with no latency SLA, and trial timings promise nothing.

options.t: Adopt the batch endpoint, and resend a change as a synchronous request when its batch result has not arrived within 45 minutes.
options.why: Incorrect. The fallback adds machinery, still risks the train, and pays full price after a 45-minute wait for any change that falls back.

options.t: Keep synchronous requests but group pending merges into one request per deploy train, scanning all of them together.
options.why: Incorrect. Packing many changes into one request dilutes attention across them; it trades accuracy for a small saving.

options.t: Keep synchronous requests for this scan, and apply the discount to work whose output is read the following day.
options.why: Correct. A 90-minute decision window needs a latency bound the Batches API does not offer, even though the job blocks no merge.

questions.decider: Each scan must be read before a train that leaves every 90 minutes; if the output were read the next day, batching with custom_id would be right.
questions.explanation: The Batches API saves 50% but has up to a 24-hour window and no latency SLA. Fit depends on whether someone waits on the result within a deadline, not on whether the job blocks a merge.

eli5.question: Should a scan that blocks nothing move to the cheaper, slower batch service? The 20-minute trial results are the bait. The clue is: on-call reads each scan before a deploy train that leaves every 90 minutes.
eli5.answer: Think of a parcel service that is half price but promises delivery only "within 24 hours". Most parcels may arrive in 20 minutes, but nothing is promised. If you need it before the 90-minute train, you pay for the courier. The Message Batches API is the cheap service: 50% off, up to 24 hours, no delivery-time guarantee (no latency SLA). Keep this scan on normal requests, and batch work nobody reads until tomorrow. Rule: if someone waits on the result by a deadline, don't batch it.
options: Runner-up. One request per change, matched back by custom_id, is a textbook batch setup. It would win if the scan were read the next day. A 90-minute deadline needs a guarantee batches don't give.
A 45-minute fallback adds moving parts. It can still miss the train, and any fallback pays full price after waiting.
Packing many merges into one request spreads the model's attention thin. Accuracy drops to save a little money.
Correct. Keep the scan on normal requests, and use the discount for work that is read the next day.

questions.question: In a nine-file merge request, the settings loader renamed retry_limit to max_retries while two consumers kept reading the old key, and review passed it. A month of post-mortems found 11 escapes of the same shape, such as a function's return tuple gaining a field while callers in sibling modules still unpacked two values. The review container starts fresh per merge request, apart from the autofix job. Each file gets its own review pass, and defects inside a single file are caught well. What change addresses the root cause?

options.t: After the file-level passes, run a pass given the changed signatures and keys, checking each against its call sites in the diff.
options.why: Correct. File-level passes cannot see contracts that span files; a separate integration pass is the multi-pass pattern for these escapes.

options.t: Add a second, independent reviewer instance per file with no access to the first reviewer's output, and merge both sets of comments.
options.why: Runner-up. Independent review beats self-review and would help if the reviewer shared context with the code's author. It already starts fresh, and a second per-file view still cannot see across files.

options.t: List shared config keys and public function signatures with their consumers in CLAUDE.md for the reviewer to load.
options.why: Incorrect. Project context helps reviews, but a hand-kept map goes stale and per-file passes still never compare two changed files.

options.t: Replace the file-level passes with one pass over the whole diff, run on a model with a larger context window.
options.why: Incorrect. One pass over many files brings back attention dilution; a larger window is not better attention.

questions.decider: Every escape spans files and the reviewer is already independent of the author; if misses sat inside single files reviewed by the authoring session, an independent instance would be the fix.
questions.explanation: Split large reviews into per-file local passes plus a cross-file integration pass. Independent instances address self-review bias, a different failure.

eli5.question: Each file is reviewed well on its own, yet bugs slip through. What is the real cause? The clue is: every escape is a mismatch between two files, and the reviewer already starts fresh, separate from the code's author.
eli5.answer: Think of checking each page of a contract on its own. Every page can be fine while page 2 and page 9 disagree. You need one more read that compares the pages against each other. That is a cross-file integration pass: it takes what changed (signatures, keys) and checks every place that uses them. Rule: per-file passes catch local bugs; a separate integration pass catches mismatches between files.
options: Correct. One more pass, after the per-file ones, that checks changed names and signatures against their callers.
Runner-up. A fresh second reviewer helps when the reviewer shares context with the author. This one already starts fresh, and still looks at one file at a time.
A hand-written map in CLAUDE.md goes stale, and the per-file passes still never compare two changed files.
One big pass over all nine files spreads attention thin. A bigger context window is not sharper attention.

questions.question: About 6% of review findings cite a line the inline-comment API rejects because it lies outside every hunk. Sampling shows most are off by exactly the hunk's starting offset: the reviewer reads the raw unified diff and counts lines from each header itself. The pre-merge budget allows one extra model call on runs that need it, but not on every run. A post step already parses hunk headers. Which TWO changes together bring rejected findings close to zero within that budget?

options.t: Route all findings through a second, independent Claude instance that confirms each cited location against the diff before posting.
options.why: Runner-up. Independent verification is sound for judgement errors, but it costs a call on every run, which the budget forbids, and reading the same raw diff it can repeat the miscount.

options.t: Prefix every line of the diff given to the reviewer with its new-file number, computed from the parsed headers.
options.why: Correct. The error is mechanical counting; supplying the numbers removes most of it at no extra call.

options.t: Compare each cited location with the parsed ranges and, for any miss, send one follow-up turn naming the finding and the valid ranges.
options.why: Correct. A deterministic check with specific feedback fixes the residue and spends the extra call only on runs that need it.

options.t: Add two sample findings to the prompt showing the correct location for a change deep inside a long hunk.
options.why: Incorrect. Samples show format, but the model would still be counting by itself, so the offset errors persist.

questions.decider: The errors are mechanical miscounts and the budget allows an extra call only when needed; if they were judgement errors and every run could afford a second call, an independent verifier would earn a place.
questions.explanation: Give the model the facts it is miscomputing, validate what it emits against them, and retry with the specific error. Spend extra calls only where validation shows they are needed.

eli5.question: Comments land on lines the code-review tool rejects. Which two changes fix it within the budget? The clue is: the errors are simple counting mistakes, and only runs that need it may spend an extra call.
eli5.answer: Think of a delivery driver who counts house numbers by hand from the corner and keeps getting it wrong. First, paint the numbers on the doors: give the model the line numbers instead of making it count. Then check each address before delivery and send the driver back once with the exact mistake (validate, then retry with specific feedback). The second step spends a call only when something fails. Rule: give the model the facts it keeps miscomputing, then check its output and retry with the exact error.
options: Runner-up. A second checker is useful for judgement calls. It costs a call on every run, which the budget forbids, and reading the same raw diff it can miscount too.
Correct. Printing each line's number removes the counting, so most errors never happen.
Correct. A plain code check catches the rest, and one targeted follow-up fixes them only when needed.
Samples show the format, but the model would still be counting by itself, so the same offset mistakes return.

questions.question: The coordinator runs the same chain on every packet: base lease, then amendments in filename order, then a reconcile step. Filename order differs from execution order in over half of packets, and that is the most common cause of wrong rent schedules. Packets hold anywhere from no amendments to eleven. In about a quarter, an amendment cites an exhibit or side letter missing from the upload, which must be requested with fetch_exhibit and may itself amend further terms. Which decomposition fits these packets best?

options.t: Sort the documents by execution date before the chain runs, and add a final integration pass that reconciles every field across all extractions.
options.why: Runner-up. A date-sorted chain with an integration pass fixes the most common error and suits packets whose contents are known up front. It has no step for retrieving documents that only surface mid-read.

options.t: Run one subagent per uploaded document in parallel, with the coordinator combining their outputs field by field into a single abstract.
options.why: Incorrect. Parallel per-document work covers only what was uploaded and cannot follow a reference to a document that has not been retrieved.

options.t: Let the coordinator plan from a first read of what each document changes and cites, adding retrieval and extraction subtasks as references surface.
options.why: Correct. Adaptive decomposition generates subtasks from what is discovered, which these packets need when references lead to documents that must be fetched.

options.t: Split the base lease into per-section passes followed by a combined pass, then apply each amendment as a patch on that result.
options.why: Incorrect. Per-section plus integration passes suit long single documents; they do not decide which amendments or exhibits govern, or fetch missing ones.

questions.decider: A quarter of packets cite documents that must be fetched and can change further terms; if every packet arrived complete, a date-sorted chain with a reconciliation pass would serve.
questions.explanation: Use fixed prompt chains for predictable inputs and adaptive decomposition when the subtasks depend on what is found along the way.

eli5.question: How should the system split up the work on lease packets that vary a lot? Filename order is the vivid cause. The clue is: a quarter of packets refer to documents that aren't there yet and must be fetched, and those can change more terms.
eli5.answer: Think of a detective case file. A fixed checklist ("read file 1, then 2, then 3") breaks when file 2 says "see the letter in the bank vault". A good detective reads first, notes what points where, then plans the next steps, including fetching the vault letter. That is adaptive decomposition: subtasks are created from what is discovered. Rule: fixed steps for predictable inputs; plan as you go when the inputs reveal new work.
options: Runner-up. Sorting by date and adding a final check fixes the most common error. It would win if every packet arrived complete. It has no step for fetching missing documents.
Reading every uploaded document in parallel covers only what was uploaded. It can't follow a pointer to a missing exhibit.
Correct. Read first, map what each document changes and points to, then add fetch and extract tasks as needed.
Section-by-section passes suit one long document. They don't decide which amendment wins or fetch missing papers.

questions.question: Five extraction subagents launch together from one coordinator response. The rent-schedule subagent converts terms like "Lease Year 3" into calendar dates, which depends on the commencement date; that date is usually set in a separate commencement memorandum, and in 14% of packets the rent subagent misses the memorandum and guesses. The term subagent, which reads the memorandum anyway, gets the date right in 99% of packets. The rent work needs that one value once per packet. Which change fits best?

options.t: Give the rent subagent a narrowly scoped find_commencement_date tool for the memorandum, keeping all five subagents in one concurrent round.
options.why: Runner-up. A scoped cross-role tool suits a frequent need during a task. Here one value is needed once, and another subagent already finds it reliably; a second lookup duplicates work and can disagree.

options.t: Sequence term before rent, with the coordinator writing the established start date into the rent task's brief.
options.why: Correct. Subagents do not inherit context; the coordinator passes the prior finding explicitly and serialises only the dependent pair.

options.t: Add the memorandum layouts seen so far to the rent subagent's system prompt, with annotated samples marking where the date appears.
options.why: Incorrect. Few-shot samples would improve the rent subagent's own search but still duplicate a value the term subagent already finds 99% of the time.

options.t: After both finish, check each rent schedule against the term subagent's date and rerun the rent subagent with the mismatch described.
options.why: Incorrect. Retry-with-feedback recovers, but it reruns 14% of rent tasks to deliver a value that could have been passed in up front.

questions.decider: The rent work needs one reliably found value once per packet; if it needed many lookups during its work, a scoped tool would win.
questions.explanation: Subagents have isolated context, so the coordinator must pass prior findings in the prompt. Serialise only true dependencies and keep independent work parallel.

eli5.question: One worker needs a date that another worker reliably finds. How should it get it? The clue is: the rent work needs that one value once per packet, and the term worker gets it right 99% of the time.
eli5.answer: Think of a kitchen. The pastry chef needs the oven temperature that the head chef already set. The manager just tells the pastry chef, rather than sending them to measure it again. Helpers (subagents) don't share memory, so the coordinator must hand over the fact in the task brief (explicit context passing). Only the two linked jobs run in order; the rest stay parallel. Rule: subagents know only what you put in their prompt.
options: Runner-up. A small dedicated lookup tool is good when a helper needs a fact often during its work. Here it needs one value once, and finding it twice can give two answers.
Correct. Run the term work first, then pass its date into the rent task. Everything else stays parallel.
Better layout samples help the rent worker search, but it still repeats work another worker already does well.
Checking afterwards and rerunning works, but it repeats 14% of rent jobs to deliver a date you could hand over at the start.

questions.question: About 90 packets a week land in the paralegal queue, chosen by calibrated field-level thresholds. Paralegals work only in the lease-administration system and never see the agent's session. Each receives the packet PDF and a "needs review" note, and a median review takes 35 minutes, most of it spent finding which field is in doubt and where the competing figures sit across 40–140 pages. What should the agent attach to each escalation?

options.t: The confidence score for every extracted value, sorted lowest first, with the PDF pages behind the lowest-scoring values highlighted.
options.why: Incorrect. Calibrated confidence is the right tool for routing, which is already done; scores point at pages but show neither the candidates nor what was checked.

options.t: A source map for every extracted value giving the document and page it came from, shown beside the abstract on the review screen.
options.why: Runner-up. Claim-to-source mapping is valuable provenance and would win if reviewers re-verified whole abstracts. They need the disputed items, the rival values and a proposal, which a full map buries.

options.t: The case-facts block the agent maintained during the run, holding amounts, dates and parties exactly as extracted, pasted into the note.
options.why: Incorrect. A case-facts block protects the agent's own context; it records what was extracted, not what is disputed or why.

options.t: A short structured brief: packet identifier, the disputed items, candidate values with document and page, checks run, and a proposed resolution.
options.why: Correct. A structured handoff lets a reviewer without the session act at once.

questions.decider: Reviewers lack the session and spend their time locating the disputed item; if they had to re-verify every value, a full source map would be the better attachment.
questions.explanation: When escalating to humans without the transcript, compile a structured handoff: identifiers, the specific issue, evidence with locations, what was tried, and the recommended action.

eli5.question: What should a human reviewer receive when the agent gives up on a packet? The clue is: reviewers never see the agent's session, and most of their 35 minutes goes on finding what is in doubt.
eli5.answer: Think of a hospital shift change. The next nurse doesn't get the whole night's recording; they get a short card: patient, problem, what was tried, what to do next. That card is a structured handoff: packet ID, the disputed items, each candidate value with document and page, checks run, and a suggested answer. The reviewer can act at once. Rule: hand humans a short structured brief, not raw data.
options: Confidence scores are for deciding who goes to review, and that is already done. They point at pages but don't show the rival values or what was checked.
Runner-up. Showing where every value came from is useful. It would win if reviewers had to recheck the whole abstract. They need the few disputed items, which a full map buries.
A case-facts block is the agent's own notepad. It lists what was extracted, not what is in doubt or why.
Correct. A short brief naming the problem, the evidence with page numbers, and a proposed answer.

questions.question: The schema's renewal_option field is an enum: fixed_rent, fair_market, cpi_linked, none. Auditors found that 7% of abstracts claim fair_market where the lease says something else, which the team is calling fabrication. In those leases the clause reads, for example, "the greater of prevailing market rent or 105% of the expiring rent" or "rent fixed by an appointed surveyor". Renewal terms are negotiated lease by lease. What schema change represents these leases best?

options.t: Add an other member alongside a free-text renewal_basis_detail holding the mechanism in the lease's own words.
options.why: Correct. The clauses state a clear mechanism outside the categories; an extensible value plus a detail field records it instead of coercing it.

options.t: Allow null for renewal_option, and instruct the model to emit null where no listed value matches the clause.
options.why: Runner-up. Nullable fields prevent fabrication when the document lacks the information. Here the clause is present and explicit, so null throws it away.

options.t: Add an unclear member with a renewal_note string, for clauses whose renewal mechanism cannot be read with confidence.
options.why: Incorrect. unclear is for ambiguous text; these clauses are clear, just outside the list, so they would be mislabelled.

options.t: Keep the four members, and add two to four annotated clauses to the prompt showing how mixed mechanisms map onto them.
options.why: Incorrect. Few-shot helps consistency, but no listed value is correct for these mechanisms, so it only standardises the wrong mapping.

questions.decider: The clauses state a definite mechanism that none of the four values covers; if the lease said nothing about renewal rent, a nullable field would be right.
questions.explanation: Use nullable fields when the source lacks the information, unclear when the text is ambiguous, and other plus a detail field when a clear value falls outside the categories.

eli5.question: A category list is missing some real answers, so the model forces a wrong one. What schema change fits? "Fabrication" tempts you toward allowing null. The clue is: these clauses clearly state how rent is set, just in terms the list doesn't include.
eli5.answer: Think of a form with tick boxes for "tea, coffee, juice" when the guest clearly asked for hot chocolate. Leaving it blank loses the order; ticking coffee is wrong. Add an "other" box with a line to write it in (an other enum value plus a detail field). Null is for when the guest said nothing at all. Rule: null for missing information, other plus detail for a clear answer outside the list.
options: Correct. An "other" choice with the lease's own wording records the real mechanism instead of forcing it into a wrong box.
Runner-up. Null is right when the lease says nothing about renewal rent. Here the clause is present and clear, so null throws it away.
"Unclear" is for text you can't read with confidence. These clauses are perfectly clear, just outside the list.
Samples make the model consistent, but no listed value is correct here, so you'd only standardise a wrong answer.

questions.question: A Pydantic validator recomputes each year of the rent schedule from the clause's base rent and escalation. On a mismatch the pipeline resends the original request with "Output failed validation. Try again." and allows five attempts. Only 31% pass on the second attempt, and one packet used all five. The lease's rent table puts base rent and CAM reimbursement in adjacent columns, and the escalation steps on each anniversary of commencement rather than each January. Which change most improves the second-attempt pass rate?

options.t: Send packets that fail the rent check to the paralegal queue with the schedule attached, and stop automatic resubmission for that check.
options.why: Runner-up. Resubmission cannot recover information absent from the source, and this would win if the figures were missing. They are in the table, so an informed retry can fix them.

options.t: Add calculated_annual_rent beside stated_annual_rent per year, with a conflict_detected flag for the model to fill.
options.why: Incorrect. Self-check fields surface conflicts in the output; the validator already detects them, and the model still is not told what went wrong.

options.t: Return the checker's specifics on the follow-up: which lease year disagreed, the figure produced, and the figure the clause implies.
options.why: Correct. Appending the specific error tells the model where to look and what to correct.

options.t: Add two annotated rent tables to the prompt, showing the base column chosen over adjacent charges and anniversary-based steps.
options.why: Incorrect. Few-shot may lift first-attempt accuracy, but the retry still says only "try again", so second attempts stay blind.

questions.decider: The correct figures are in the lease's table, so a retry can succeed if told what failed; if they were absent, routing to a human would be right.
questions.explanation: Retry-with-error-feedback appends the specific validation failure. It works for misreads and format errors, not for information missing from the document.

eli5.question: Retries after a failed rent check rarely work. What makes the second try succeed? The clue is: the right numbers are in the lease, in a column next to a similar one, and the steps follow anniversaries, not January.
eli5.answer: Think of a teacher handing back homework marked only "wrong, try again". The student guesses. If the teacher writes "year 3 should be 41,200, you wrote 46,900", the student finds the mistake fast. That is retry with specific error feedback. It works because the answer is in the lease. If it were missing, no retry would help. Rule: when retrying, say exactly what failed.
options: Runner-up. Sending to a human is right when the information isn't in the document. Here it is, so an informed retry can fix it.
Self-check fields show conflicts, but the validator already finds them. The model still isn't told what went wrong.
Correct. Tell the model which year failed, what it produced, and what the clause implies.
Samples may improve the first try, but the retry still just says "try again", so second tries stay blind.

questions.question: Each document in a packet is sent alone to an extraction request offering extract_lease, extract_amendment and extract_guaranty. Uploads carry no type label. With tool_choice on auto, about 4% of responses are prose, such as "This appears to be a personal guaranty of the tenant's obligations…", and the parser drops them. In an audit of 1,000 responses that did call a tool, the tool matched the document type every time. What is the best fix?

options.t: Expand each extractor's description with distinguishing features and sample headings for its document type.
options.why: Incorrect. Better descriptions improve selection, which the audit shows is already right; they do not stop text replies.

options.t: Add a first call that labels the document type, then name the matching extractor in a forced tool_choice.
options.why: Runner-up. Classify-then-force is right when the model picks the wrong tool. Selection is already correct, so the extra call buys nothing that requiring a call does not.

options.t: Leave auto in place and, when stop_reason is end_turn, resend with a note that a tool call is required.
options.why: Incorrect. Detecting and resending recovers the 4% at the cost of a second call each, when the API can require a call on the first.

options.t: Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} on every extraction call and keep the three schemas unchanged.
options.why: Correct. any requires a tool call and leaves the choice to the model, which already chooses well.

questions.decider: When the model calls a tool it picks correctly every time, so only text replies fail; if it picked the wrong extractor, classifying first and forcing a named tool would be better.
questions.explanation: auto may return text, any requires some tool call, and a forced tool requires one specific tool. Use any when the right tool is not known in advance.

eli5.question: Sometimes the model answers in prose instead of calling an extraction tool. What is the smallest correct fix? The clue is: when it does call a tool, it always picks the right one.
eli5.answer: Think of a receptionist who always sends visitors to the right desk, but sometimes just chats instead of sending them anywhere. You don't need a new sorting step; you need a rule: "every visitor goes to some desk". In the API that is tool_choice: {"type": "any"}: the model must call a tool but still chooses which one. Rule: auto may chat, any must call a tool, forced must call that specific tool.
options: Better descriptions improve which desk is chosen, and that is already right. They don't stop the chatting.
Runner-up. Labelling first and forcing a named tool is right when the model picks the wrong tool. It already picks correctly, so the extra call buys nothing.
Detecting chat and resending recovers the answer, but costs a second call when the API can require a tool call the first time.
Correct. Require a tool call and let the model keep choosing which one.

questions.trap: More context or reasoning instead of structure
questions.question: Each abstract carries a non_standard_clauses list for the legal team, produced from the instruction "list any unusual or non-standard clauses". In one abstract a co-tenancy right sat 27th in a list of 31 items, most of them routine assignment and repair language. Across a month, 65% of listed items were routine. Legal's playbook defines non-standard as five clause families, each with trigger language. The list format is consistent. What change most improves precision?

options.t: Add three annotated leases to the prompt marking which provisions belonged on the list and which routine ones were left off.
options.why: Runner-up. Few-shot samples help where the boundary is hard to put into words or format varies. The playbook already states the boundary, and the format is fine.

options.t: Replace the open-ended wording with a closed set of categories and their qualifying phrasing, treating the rest as routine.
options.why: Correct. Explicit categorical criteria are the main lever for precision; vague "unusual" wording produces false positives.

options.t: Tag each listed item with a detected_pattern and track which tags legal dismisses, then prune the noisiest tags.
options.why: Incorrect. Dismissal tracking discovers unknown noise sources; the definition of a correct item already exists and can be applied now.

options.t: Have a second, independent Claude instance review each list and drop items it judges routine before legal receives it.
options.why: Incorrect. An independent filter applying the same vague notion of "routine" inherits the ambiguity, at double the cost.

questions.decider: Legal's playbook already defines the categories in words; if the boundary could not be stated, few-shot samples would be the strongest lever.
questions.explanation: Precision comes from explicit categorical criteria. Few-shot samples complement criteria for consistency and hard cases; review layers do not fix a vague definition.

eli5.question: A "list unusual clauses" output is full of routine items. How do you make it precise? The buried co-tenancy right is the vivid detail. The clue is: legal's playbook already defines the five kinds that count.
eli5.answer: Think of telling a library volunteer to pull "interesting books". You get a cartful. Give them the five shelf codes you actually want and you get exactly those. Replacing a vague word with a closed list of categories and their trigger wording is explicit categorical criteria, the main lever for precision. Rule: if you can write the categories down, write them down.
options: Runner-up. Worked samples help when the boundary is hard to put into words. Here legal has already put it into words.
Correct. Use only the defined categories and their trigger phrasing; everything else is routine.
Tracking which items legal dismisses finds unknown causes of noise. The definition already exists and can be used now.
A second checker using the same vague idea of "routine" makes the same vague calls, at twice the cost.

questions.question: The escalation object has type (fixed_pct, fixed_amount, cpi, stepped) plus floor_pct, cap_pct and steps; legal has confirmed every clause seen so far fits it. The prompt defines each type and where floors and caps go. Hybrid clauses such as "CPI, not below 2% or above 5%" or "the greater of 3% or CPI" are encoded differently across runs, sometimes as cpi with bounds, sometimes as fixed_pct with a bound dropped. Reviewers reject 18% of escalations. What is the most effective next step?

options.t: Work three mixed-mechanism clauses through in the prompt, each with its expected JSON and a line on why that category applies.
options.why: Correct. When the schema fits and written definitions still give inconsistent results, a few worked cases showing the reasoning are the most effective fix.

options.t: Add an other type with an escalation_detail string, and route those escalations to paralegals for manual entry.
options.why: Runner-up. An other-plus-detail value is right when clauses fall outside the schema. Legal confirms they fit, so this sends structured data to manual entry.

options.t: Split into two calls: classify the type first, then extract bounds and steps with a prompt specific to that type.
options.why: Incorrect. Prompt chaining isolates steps, but the inconsistency is the type decision itself, which the first call would repeat.

options.t: Recompute three years of rent from each escalation and, on a mismatch with the lease, retry with the discrepancy described.
options.why: Incorrect. CPI-linked rent cannot be recomputed from the lease alone, so the check cannot tell a right hybrid encoding from a wrong one.

questions.decider: The schema already represents every clause and only the mapping varies; if clauses fell outside the schema, an other-plus-detail value would be right.
questions.explanation: Few-shot cases, including ambiguous ones with the reasoning shown, are the most effective way to get consistent output when instructions alone are inconsistent.

eli5.question: Mixed escalation clauses come out differently on different runs. What is the best next step? The clue is: legal confirms every clause fits the existing format, and the prompt already defines each type.
eli5.answer: Think of teaching someone to file mixed receipts. The rules are written down, yet they file tricky ones differently each time. Walk them through three tricky receipts, showing where each goes and why. Worked cases that show the reasoning (few-shot examples) are the strongest fix when written rules alone give inconsistent results. Rule: when definitions exist but tricky cases vary, show worked cases.
options: Correct. Three tricky clauses with the expected output and a one-line reason teach the mapping.
Runner-up. An "other" box is right when clauses don't fit the format. Legal says they all fit, so this pushes good data into manual entry.
Splitting into two calls keeps the hard decision, choosing the type, in the first call. The same inconsistency repeats there.
Future CPI isn't in the lease, so recomputing rent can't tell a right encoding from a wrong one.

questions.question: The same premises often show several rents across a packet: $38.50 per square foot in the base lease, $41.00 in a 2021 amendment, $39.75 in a side letter. Reviewers log these as conflicts, and reconciliation keeps whichever figure its prompt finds most authoritative, discarding the others. Each amendment and side letter states the date it takes effect; the side letter was signed after the amendment but takes effect before it. What should reconciliation do with these figures?

options.t: Mark the field as disputed, store each rent with its source and page, and send the packet to a paralegal to choose the current figure.
options.why: Runner-up. Annotating conflicts with sources rather than picking one is right for a real contradiction, such as two values in force at once. These are successive values, and their dates order them.

options.t: Set a conflict_detected flag, keep the rent from the most recently signed document as current, and log the other values.
options.why: Incorrect. Signing order is not effect order: the side letter was signed last but took effect before the amendment.

options.t: Run a second, independent extraction over the three documents and keep the rent both passes judge most authoritative.
options.why: Incorrect. Agreement between passes still discards the other values and never uses the dates.

options.t: Store each rent with source, page and effective date, take the current figure from the latest one, and keep the rest as history.
options.why: Correct. Capturing dates with attribution shows a sequence over time, not contradictions, and keeps provenance for every value.

questions.decider: Each document states when it takes effect, so the values form a sequence; if they lacked dates or applied at the same time, flagging the conflict for a person would be correct.
questions.explanation: Keep claim-to-source mappings through synthesis and capture dates so temporal differences are not misread as contradictions. Real conflicts get annotated with sources, not resolved arbitrarily.

eli5.question: Three documents show three different rents. Is that a conflict? Reviewers call it one, which is the bait. The clue is: each document states when it takes effect, and the side letter was signed last but took effect earlier.
eli5.answer: Think of a price board in a shop over the years: £38.50, then £39.75, then £41.00. Those aren't three competing prices; they're a history. Record each value with its source, page and effective date, take today's price from the latest effective date, and keep the rest as history (source attribution with dates). A real conflict would be two prices in force at once. Rule: check the dates before calling it a contradiction.
options: Runner-up. Flagging with sources is right for a true conflict, two values in force at the same time. These follow each other, and their dates order them.
Signing date isn't effect date. The side letter was signed last but took effect first, so this picks the wrong rent.
Two passes agreeing still throws the other values away and never looks at the dates.
Correct. Keep every value with its source and effective date, and take the current rent from the latest one.

questions.question: On a labelled set of 2,000 packets, field-level accuracy is 97%, and the business plans to let some abstracts post without paralegal review from launch next month. US office leases make up 82% of the set; UK retail and ground leases make up the rest. Compliance requires a measured error rate under 1% for any field that skips review, from the first abstract posted. The model returns a per-field confidence value. Which TWO together meet that requirement at launch?

options.t: Break the results out by document type and by field, and let only type-field pairs under the error bar bypass review.
options.why: Correct. A 97% aggregate can hide weak lease types or fields; measuring each pair is what shows which can skip review.

options.t: Sample auto-posted abstracts weekly with stratification by lease type, and track the measured error rate for each stratum.
options.why: Runner-up. Stratified sampling of production output is the right ongoing monitor. It only measures abstracts that have already posted, so it cannot qualify anything on day one.

options.t: Fit each field's confidence cut-off on the labelled set, and send any value scoring under its cut-off to a paralegal.
options.why: Correct. Confidence calibrated on labelled data routes individual doubtful values to review.

options.t: Recompute totals from each rent schedule, and route any abstract whose stated and calculated totals disagree to review.
options.why: Incorrect. A self-consistency check catches some errors but measures no error rate, and most fields have no total to check.

questions.decider: The error rate must be measured before the first post, which only the labelled set allows; after launch, stratified sampling of posted abstracts would be the ongoing check.
questions.explanation: Aggregate accuracy masks weak segments. Before automating, validate by document type and field and calibrate field-level confidence on labelled data; after launch, monitor with stratified sampling.

eli5.question: Which two steps prove, before launch, which fields can skip human review? The clue is: the error rate must be measured from the very first posted abstract, and only the labelled set exists before launch.
eli5.answer: Think of a restaurant inspection before opening day. You test each dish on its own, not just an average score. You also check how well the chef's "I'm sure" matches reality. Break accuracy down by lease type and field, and tune each field's confidence cut-off on the labelled set (calibration). Spot-checking real orders comes after opening. Rule: before automating, validate by segment and calibrate on labelled data; after launch, sample.
options: Correct. A 97% average can hide weak lease types or fields. Measuring each pair shows which can skip review.
Runner-up. Stratified spot-checks of live output are the right ongoing monitor. They need posted abstracts, so they can't qualify anything on day one.
Correct. Confidence tuned on labelled data sends just the doubtful values to a person.
A totals check catches some errors but measures no error rate, and most fields have no total to check.
